1. Core Clinical Tension: A 62-year-old woman with a 3-year history of chronic pruritic skin lesions was initially misdiagnosed with thyroid-related dermatosis and later idiopathic erythroderma. Protracted courses of potent topical corticosteroids and systemic prednisone suppressed cutaneous cell-mediated immunity and blunted typical inflammatory reactions, permitting uncontrolled mite hyperinfestation. The resulting extensive hyperkeratotic, crusted erythroderma closely mimicked severe psoriasis, eczema, or cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Admission triage concludes after documenting the 3-year history of refractory erythrodermic plaques under corticosteroid therapy, physical exam demonstrating generalized scaling erythroderma, thick hyperkeratotic plaques, crusted scalp and ear lesions, fever, and triage laboratory results (elevated ESR 46 mm/hr, leukocytosis with eosinophilia 1.3 x 10^9/L, normal renal/hepatic/glucose/urinalysis panels), immediately prior to skin scraping microscopy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Endocrine-associated dermatosis secondary to long-standing hypothyroidism was initially suspected but did not respond to thyroid management or topical steroids. Idiopathic erythroderma / severe eczema was entertained and repeatedly biopsied (showing only non-specific inflammation), but systemic corticosteroids caused dependence with rebound flaring upon tapering.
case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman presented to the hospital with widespread, severe skin eruptions that had acutely worsened over the preceding few weeks. Her dermatologic history began 3 years earlier with diffuse erythematous, slightly infiltrated plaques on her trunk and extremities without sharp demarcation, accompanied by moderate pruritus. Due to a 20-year history of treated hypothyroidism, her initial skin lesions were attributed to an endocrine-related cutaneous disorder. Over 5 months, repeated courses of potent topical corticosteroids (betamethasone valerate 0.1%, triamcinolone acetonide 0.1%, fluocinonide 0.05%) provided no improvement. Over the subsequent 6 months, her cutaneous lesions progressed into generalized scaling erythroderma with persistent, severe pruritus. Systemic corticosteroid therapy (prednisone 20–40 mg daily) was maintained for nearly a year; lesions transiently improved but flared consistently whenever the steroid dose was tapered. Multiple skin biopsies performed during that period revealed only non-specific inflammatory changes.

On physical examination, the patient had an elevated body temperature and was febrile. Dermatologic evaluation revealed generalized erythema and scaling involving the face and entire body, large hyperkeratotic plaques on the trunk and limbs, and thick crusted lesions covering the scalp and external ears. Pruritus was severe and intractable, preventing sleep.

Triage laboratory investigations revealed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 46 mm/hr and leukocytosis with eosinophilia (1.3 × 10^9/L). Routine hematologic parameters (urea, creatinine, liver enzymes, glucose) and urinalysis were within normal limits.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Initially considered due to a 20-year medical history of hypothyroidism, but skin lesions were completely unresponsive to potent topical corticosteroids and progressed into generalized erythroderma.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Because she had been suffered from hypothyroidosis for 20 yr, at the first dermatological examination, she was misdiagnosed and her skin changes were thought to be in relation with the endocrine disorder.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Diagnosed when scaling plaques generalized; repeated skin biopsies demonstrated only non-specific inflammation, but medium-to-high dose systemic corticosteroid therapy led to rebound flares on dose reduction and masked an underlying parasitic infestation.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Biopsy specimens were taken several times, but on microscopic examination there were only signs of nonspecific inflammation.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Clinical suspicion of crusted (Norwegian) scabies prompted direct microscopic examination of skin scrapings from hyperkeratotic trunk lesions, which revealed overwhelming numbers of mites and eggs.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: At this time crusted scabies was suspected and microscopical examination of scrapings from the hyperkeratotic lesions from trunk (we did not examined tips of fingers and toes) showed numerous mites and eggs (Fig. 3).

editor_comments: A severe case of crusted (Norwegian) scabies precipitated by long-term topical and systemic corticosteroid administration for misdiagnosed erythroderma, culminating in hospital transmission to 7 staff members and 14 fellow inpatients.
